edges.justification: Book‑to‑market ratio is measured at the start of the year and reflects the firm’s valuation; a higher ratio often signals constrained growth and thus influences the firm’s annual return.
Earnings surprise occurs during the year and directly impacts the stock’s performance, thereby driving the annual return.
Firm performance influences institutional investor appetite; better or worse returns can trigger changes in institutional ownership.
Higher leverage increases financial risk and can depress future returns, so leverage at the start of the year influences the annual return.
The market’s aggregate return is a key driver of systematic risk and therefore influences the individual firm’s return.
Historical performance often predicts future returns through momentum; past five‑year return therefore informs the current annual return.
Valuation ratios influence analysts’ forecasts and expectations, thereby affecting the magnitude of earnings surprise.
Valuation signals impact institutional investors’ decisions; a higher book‑to‑market ratio can attract or deter institutional ownership.
Higher debt relative to equity reduces market value, increasing the book‑to‑market ratio.
Past performance influences market valuation, which in turn affects the book‑to‑market ratio.
The book‑to‑market ratio contributes to the safety component of the quality score.
Membership in a value index is largely determined by the book‑to‑market ratio.
Unexpected earnings can alter institutional investor sentiment and ownership decisions.
Leverage can influence earnings volatility, which affects the magnitude of the earnings surprise.
Significant earnings surprises can shift market sentiment, thereby influencing the market return.
Historical performance informs forecasts; better past performance can lead to smaller surprises.
Earnings surprise contributes to the profitability component of the quality score.
Value‑style firms often exhibit distinct earnings patterns, influencing the surprise magnitude.
Leverage affects the firm’s risk profile, which can influence institutional ownership changes.
Market performance drives institutional investor allocation decisions.
Past performance informs investor confidence and thus ownership changes.
Higher quality attracts institutional investors, leading to ownership changes.
Value index membership attracts certain institutional investors, affecting ownership.
Higher leverage reduces the safety component of the quality score.
Market conditions influence profitability, which is part of the quality score.
Historical performance informs the quality assessment.
Being a value‑index member is associated with higher future returns.
QualityScore is calculated at the end of the year using the firm's annual return and other fundamentals, so the annual return influences the quality score, not the other way around.
